steps.title: Four sentences about money.
steps.sub: Notice the word before the noun each time.

items.text: I have a few good shirts.
I spend a lot of money on the gym.

steps.title: Look at the four sentences again.
steps.sub: much money · a few shirts · a lot of money
steps.prompt: Why is it much money but a few shirts?
options: Money is uncountable; shirts are countable.
Because money is more important than shirts.
Because the first sentence is negative.
steps.answer: Money is uncountable; shirts are countable.
steps.why: Much and a little go with uncountable nouns; many and a few go with countable plurals.

steps.title: How much? How many?
steps.html:
Countable (shirts, coins)Uncountable (money, time)
a small amounta few shirtsa little money
a large amounta lot of / lots of coinsa lot of / lots of money
questionHow many coins?How much money?
negativenot many coinsnot much money
more than you wanttoo many billstoo much money
the right amountenough shirtsenough money

Much and many are most natural in questions and negatives: How much is the rent? I don’t have many coins. In positive sentences use a lot of.

Some in positive sentences, any in negatives and questions: I still buy some coffees. There isn’t any money left. Have you got any change?

Enough comes before a noun but after an adjective: enough money, but the flat isn’t big enough.

Too much / too many means more than you want. It is not the same as very: It’s very expensive ≠ It costs too much.

You will use a lot of and not enough again in Unit 11, when you talk about global problems.

steps.title: You are going to read about three people and their money.
steps.sub: Which of these do you think all three of them say? There is no wrong answer here.

steps.title: Three people and their money
steps.html:
One spends on one thing. One counts. One waits.

Reading

Nurlan, 24. “I don’t have much money and I don’t need much. My rent is low because I share with three people. I have a few good shirts and one pair of shoes. I spend a lot of money on one thing only: the gym. It costs too much, everybody says so, but it is the only place where I stop thinking about work.”

Dina, 39. “I earn enough, but there is never any money left at the end of the month. For years I didn’t know where it went. Then I started writing everything down for thirty days. I found a lot of small things — a few coffees a day, a little money here and there, one taxi a week — and together they were more than my electricity bill. I still buy some coffees. But I know how many.”

Aset, 61. “I never borrowed money in my life, and I never used a credit card. My children think that is strange. They say I don’t have enough information about modern life, and perhaps that is true. But I don’t owe anybody anything, and at my age that is worth more than a lot of things you can buy.”

Three people, three answers. Nurlan spends on one thing. Dina counts. Aset waits.

None of them has a lot of money. All three of them say the same sentence: “I have enough.”

steps.sub: Six sentences. Use a different quantifier in each one.
steps.placeholder: I spend a lot of money on …
steps.html:
1. Plan: what you spend a lot on → what you spend very little on → what costs too much → what you don’t have enough of → what you are saving up for.
  • I spend a lot of money on …
